tour.title: Intramuros: The Walled City
tour.summary: Six stops inside Manila's 16th-century walled city — a Spanish fort and the cell where José Rizal wrote his farewell poem, the colonial square, the cathedral, a grand colonial house, the oldest stone church in the country, and the southern bastion where the walls end.
tour.overviewText:
Manila greets you in early April as heat and noise. Step out at dawn and the city is already working — jeepneys, the converted American military jeeps that serve as the country's buses, threading the traffic; vendors setting up; church bells. By nine the sun is a weight. This walk is built for that clock: get inside the old walls early, before the day turns brutal.

What you are walking into is the heart of a vanished empire. On 24 June 1571 the Spanish conquistador Miguel López de Legazpi founded his capital on the site of Maynila, a Muslim Tagalog settlement at the mouth of the Pasig River whose chief, Rajah Sulayman, had just been defeated. That pre-colonial Manila already traded with China, Borneo and the Malay world; the Spanish took the crossroads and made it imperial. Intramuros — Latin for "within the walls" — became the capital of the Spanish East Indies, governed not from Madrid but from Mexico City, and the walled city was the empire's Asian headquarters for government, the Church, schools and money.

The money came from the Manila galleons. From 1565 to 1815, one or two great ships a year crossed the Pacific between Manila and Acapulco, carrying Chinese silk and porcelain one way and New World silver the other. For two and a half centuries this was the only regular link between Asia and the Americas — an early trade route to circle the planet. The ships were built and largely crewed by Filipinos. When the last galleon sailed in 1815, the city had already been shaped by what the trade left behind: stone churches, a Chinese merchant quarter across the river, and a Spanish-speaking elite.

Two things you should hold before you start. First, faith: the Philippines is Asia's largest Christian nation, and roughly four in five Filipinos are Catholic. The Augustinian friars who landed with Legazpi in 1565 ran the parishes and much of local government; their wealth and power were among the grievances that lit the 1896 revolution against Spain, whose national hero, José Rizal, was shot just outside these walls. Second, catastrophe: in February and March 1945, the Battle of Manila levelled the walled city and killed at least 100,000 civilians — the worst urban fighting American forces fought in the Pacific. Intramuros was reduced to rubble. One church survived.

The walk runs roughly south from the fort at the river mouth to the great southern bastion: fort, colonial square, cathedral, a grand colonial house, the oldest stone church in the country, then the walls themselves. It is short — barely a kilometre and a half of walking — but dense, and the fort interior and two museums will fill a morning.

Practicals: fees are in Philippine pesos (₱); most sites open around 8 or 9am and the fort stays open late. Hours and prices move, so verify at every gate. Bring water and a hat — there are few shaded sidewalks, the streets are shared with traffic, and the April heat is real. If you have a second day, Rizal Park and the National Museum complex sit just outside the walls.

Start at the gate with the wooden saint on it.
tour.difficulty: Easy to moderate. The route is flat, but it is sun-exposed, the old streets often have no sidewalk and are shared with cars, and the fort, walls and museum upper floors have steps, cobbles and uneven stone.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Early morning, ideally at opening — Fort Santiago opens at 6am at weekends and 8am on weekdays — to beat both the heat and the tour buses. Finish by late morning; April is the hottest month of the year, so carry water and plan to sit out the early afternoon.

stops.name: Fort Santiago & the Rizal Shrine
stops.narration:
You are standing at the mouth of the Pasig River, on the oldest military ground in Manila. Look up at the gate: the wooden relief shows Santiago Matamoros, Saint James the Moor-slayer, the warrior-saint the Spanish made their patron, riding down his enemies. The fort is named for him, and the name is a mission statement. Spain came here to conquer, and it built in stone so the conquest would stay.

Before the Spanish, this tongue of land between the river and the bay was Maynila, a fortified trading settlement ruled by Rajah Sulayman, a Muslim Tagalog chief whose bronze swivel guns were cast by Panday Pira, a famous smith from Mindanao. It traded with China, Borneo and the Malay world. Legazpi's forces took it in 1571; in 1574 a Chinese warlord, Limahong, burned the first wooden fort down, and that decided the Spanish: they rebuilt in stone. The citadel you are inside went up between 1590 and 1593 under Governor-General Gómez Pérez Dasmariñas, built of volcanic tuff quarried at Guadalupe — a place you now know as Makati.

For three centuries this was a prison as much as a fortress. Spanish, then British (1762–64), then American, then Japanese occupiers all used it as headquarters and jail, and the Japanese secret police, the Kempeitai, tortured prisoners here during the Second World War. Walk the plaza, the dungeons and the walls, and then find the low brick barracks on the left of Plaza de Armas. That is the Museo ni Rizal, and it matters more than anything else in the fort.

José Rizal was a doctor — an eye specialist trained in Madrid and Heidelberg — and a writer, and his two novels, Noli Me Tángere (1887) and El filibusterismo (1891), exposed the abuses of Spanish rule and helped make the 1896 revolution thinkable. He did not lead it, and disapproved of armed revolt almost to the end; it made no difference. He was arrested, tried for rebellion and held here for fifty-six days, from 3 November to 29 December 1896. In his cell he wrote a farewell poem, fourteen stanzas in Spanish, with no title and no signature. The night before his execution he told his sister Trinidad that something was in the small alcohol stove; she carried it home and found the folded paper. We know the poem as Mi último adiós, "My Last Farewell".

On the morning of 30 December 1896 he married Josephine Bracken, his Irish companion in exile, and then walked out through this gate. Bronze footsteps in the ground trace the route — through the fort, out, and along the road to Bagumbayan, the execution ground that is now Rizal Park. He was thirty-five. The firing squad did not shoot him in the back; he turned to face it, and fell facing the sky. Ask why a reformer, not an independence leader, became the national hero: because the Spanish shot him, and in doing so gave the revolution its martyr.

Two practical notes. Fort Santiago charges about ₱75 for adults and ₱50 for students, seniors and people with disabilities — verify at the gate, because rates move. It opens 8am on weekdays and 6am at weekends, and closes at 10pm with last entry at 8pm (8:30pm at weekends). The Rizal Shrine inside keeps shorter hours, roughly 8am to 5pm, Tuesday to Sunday. And near the dungeons you will find a plain white cross: it marks a mass grave of six hundred bodies found around Intramuros after the 1945 battle, the first of several reminders on this walk of what happened to this city.

When you are ready, leave by the main gate and turn left, then right onto General Luna Street, the old Calle Real del Palacio, and walk south-east about six hundred metres. The buildings open out into a small square with a bronze king on a column in the middle: Plaza de Roma.
stops.entranceFeeNote: About ₱75 for adults, ₱50 for students, seniors and people with disabilities. Rates move and can differ for foreign visitors, so verify at the gate and carry small peso notes.
stops.openingHours: Weekdays roughly 8am to 10pm, weekends from 6am, with last entry about 8pm (8:30pm at weekends). The Rizal Shrine inside keeps shorter hours, roughly 8am to 5pm, Tuesday to Sunday. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: Partly accessible at best. The entrance plaza and main paths are level, but the fort has cobbles, uneven stone, steps onto the walls and narrow dungeon passages. The Rizal Shrine has stairs between floors.
stops.insiderTip: Find the bronze footsteps near the gate and follow them the way Rizal walked on the morning of 30 December 1896. Then look for the low brick barracks on the far side of Plaza de Armas — that is the Museo ni Rizal, easily missed, and the heart of the site.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the fort by the main gate, turn left and then right onto General Luna Street, the old Calle Real del Palacio, and walk south-east for about six hundred metres. The street opens into a small square with a bronze king on a column in the middle — Plaza de Roma.

stops.name: Plaza de Roma
stops.narration:
You are standing on the plaza mayor of Spanish Manila — the civic heart of an empire's Asian capital. In the colonial centuries this small rectangle held the whole apparatus: the cathedral on one side, the Ayuntamiento, or city hall, on another, and the Palacio del Gobernador, the governor-general's residence, where the tall modern building now stands. The bronze horseman on the column is King Carlos IV of Spain, cast in 1808 and put up in 1824 by a grateful colonial government: he had sent a shipment of smallpox vaccine to the Philippines. A statue of a Spanish king, raised for a public-health favour, in the middle of a Filipino city — that is the colonial relationship in one object.

Hold the scale of what was governed from here. Intramuros was the capital of the Spanish East Indies, a realm that stretched to Guam and the Marianas, and for most of its history it was run not from Madrid but from Mexico City, through the Viceroyalty of New Spain. The governor-general ruled from inside these walls from 1571 until 1865. Then, on 3 June 1863, an earthquake destroyed the Palacio del Gobernador and much of the city, and the governor moved his residence about three kilometres up the Pasig to Malacañang — still the presidential palace today. That move is the beginning of the story this square tells: power slowly leaking out of the walls.

It left for good after 1898, when Spain, defeated in the Spanish–American War, sold the Philippines to the United States for twenty million dollars in the Treaty of Paris. The Americans raised their flag at Fort Santiago, and the Ayuntamiento became the seat of the Philippine Commission, the body that governed the colony. Under American rule the moat was drained and became a golf course, the walls were breached to let traffic through, and the shoreline was pushed out by land reclamation for the port, so a city built as a fortress by the sea found itself inland.

Modern Manila finished the job. After independence in 1946 the capital stayed here in name, but government offices, universities, banks and malls spread to Quezon City and Makati, and Metro Manila grew into a sprawl of some twenty-five million people. Quezon City is now the country's most populous city; the money is in Makati; Intramuros is a historic district of about seven thousand residents. In 1945 the square's buildings were gutted — for years the Ayuntamiento was used as a parking lot — and reconstruction here has been slow and piecemeal.

The square is free and open at all hours. Two warnings: Intramuros has few proper sidewalks, so walk facing the traffic; and the Palacio del Gobernador building is not a palace any more — it houses the Commission on Elections. When you are ready, the cathedral is about fifty metres to your south-east. Face the bronze king, turn left, and walk towards the twin towers.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free, open square. The surrounding government buildings are working offices, not sights.
stops.openingHours: Open access at all times. Best in morning or late-afternoon light, when the bronze and the façades are not in flat overhead sun.
stops.accessibility: Level paved square, step-free. The surrounding pavements and crossings are uneven and there are few marked crossings.
stops.insiderTip: The bronze statue is not a conquistador or a governor but King Carlos IV — the colonial government raised it in gratitude for a shipment of smallpox vaccine. Read the inscription; it is the strangest monument in the district.
stops.nextStopDirections: The cathedral is only about fifty metres away. Face the bronze king, turn left and walk south-east towards the twin bell towers and the Neo-Romanesque façade; the main doors face the square.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Gerswin at English Wikipedia, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Manila Cathedral
stops.narration:
This is the mother church of the Philippines: the Manila Cathedral, formally the Minor Basilica and Metropolitan Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, seat of the Archbishop of Manila. Understand the country's faith and you understand the country. The Philippines is the largest Christian nation in Asia, and roughly four out of five Filipinos are Catholic — the result of three centuries of Spanish missionary work that began when the Augustinian order landed with Legazpi in 1565. The friars did not only say Mass; they ran the parishes, the schools and much of local administration, collecting taxes and policing morals. Their power was so complete that it became one of the grievances behind the 1896 revolution — and the Church is still the most influential institution in the land.

Now look at the building and count its deaths. A church has stood on this spot since 1581, when the first cathedral was built of nipa palm, wood and bamboo. It burned, was rebuilt in stone, and was destroyed again — by the earthquake of 1600, by the earthquakes of 1645, by fire and earthquake in 1863, and by the earthquake of 1880 that toppled its bell tower. The seventh cathedral, finished in 1879, was wrecked in 1945 when Japanese troops made a scorched-earth stand in Intramuros; civilians hiding inside were killed. What you see is the eighth cathedral, consecrated in 1958, designed by the Filipino architect Fernando Ocampo in a Neo-Romanesque style that copies the façade of its lost predecessor. Even its bells have been moved: in 2011 the carillon was lowered to ground level so the tower would not collapse in the next big quake.

Step inside if the doors are open. The scale is deliberate — the nave holds two thousand people — and it is a working church, not a museum: Masses run daily, and there may be a wedding or a funeral when you arrive. Three popes have said Mass here — Paul VI in 1970, John Paul II in 1981 and Francis in 2015 — and the cathedral is dedicated to the Immaculate Conception, the doctrine that the Virgin Mary was conceived free of original sin, and she is the principal patroness of the Philippines. That belief is explained in a small exhibit in one of the side chapels near the entrance; look for it, because it is the sort of thing a visitor is too embarrassed to ask about.

Practically: entry is free, donations are welcome, and there is no ticket. The cathedral is normally open through the day outside Mass times, but hours shift with the liturgical calendar, so check at the door. Dress modestly — shoulders and knees covered is the safe rule — and keep your voice down. The floor is level and step-free.

Leave by the main doors, turn right and walk south down General Luna Street for about three hundred and fifty metres. On your left, inside a low colonial-style courtyard complex, is Casa Manila.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry; donations welcome. It is a working cathedral, not a ticketed monument.
stops.openingHours: Normally open through the day outside Mass times, roughly early morning to early evening, but hours shift with the liturgical calendar and can close for weddings and funerals. Check at the door.
stops.accessibility: Step-free and level inside, with a shallow ramp or step at the main doors. Pews and side aisles are wide enough for a wheelchair.
stops.insiderTip: Look for the small historical exhibit in a side chapel near the entrance: it explains the cathedral's eight rebuildings and the Immaculate Conception, the doctrine the church is dedicated to. Then find the cardinal's hats — the scarlet galeros — hanging from the dome.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the main doors, turn right and walk south down General Luna Street for about three hundred and fifty metres. On your left, inside a low colonial-style courtyard complex, is Casa Manila; the entrance is through the courtyard.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Markadan, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Casa Manila
stops.narration:
Casa Manila is a beautiful lie, and it tells you more than the truth would. Every stone and plank of this house is modern — it was built in the 1980s, and it is a copy of an 1850s mansion, the San Nicolas House, that once stood on Calle Jaboneros in Binondo, the Chinese quarter across the river. The architect was J. Ramon Faustmann. It is a reconstruction, in other words, of the kind of house the 1945 bombing destroyed here by the hundred, and that is exactly why it is worth an hour: it shows you the domestic world the walled city lost.

This building type is called a bahay na bato — literally a "stone house", stone below and wood above — and it was engineered for this country's three great hazards: heat, earthquakes and floods. The ground floor is heavy adobe: a wide stone passage called the zaguan for carriages and storage, an open patio to cool the rooms, stables at the back. The family lived upstairs, on timber, which flexes in a quake instead of cracking. The windows are the clever part. The panes are not glass, which was expensive, but flat translucent capiz shells; outside them are wooden louvres, the persianas, that let air move while cutting the glare; and underneath are sliding panels, the ventanillas, that a child could open to watch a procession in the street.

Walk the rooms in order and you walk a social hierarchy. On the mezzanine, the entresuelo, are the master's office and the rooms of unmarried aunts and grandparents. Upstairs, the caida is where everyday guests were received; the sala, with its European gilt furniture, chandeliers and piano, is where the family held tertulias — private evening concerts — and dances. Beside it is the oratorio, the family chapel, its altar crowded with santos, devotional statues whose heads and hands were often carved from ivory. In the dining room hangs a punkah, a ceiling fan pulled by a cord, possibly brought from India during the British occupation of 1762. At the back are the kitchen, the azotea where laundry and butchering were done, and the aljibe, the cistern that stored rainwater filtered through gravel and charcoal. Running along the window side is the volada, the narrow corridor servants used to move between rooms without crossing the family's path.

Here is the fact that reframes the elegance: the wealth that paid for the chandeliers came mostly from haciendas, large provincial estates worked by tenant farmers, and from the Chinese-Filipino trade that made Binondo rich. A tiny colonial elite lived like this while the great majority of Filipinos were tenants, labourers or servants. The land question was one of the fuses of the 1896 revolution — and the family whose house this copies belonged to the class the revolution was partly aimed at, as well as the class that led it.

Casa Manila is open Tuesday to Sunday, 9am to 6pm, with last entry at 5pm, and closed on Mondays; the ticket is about ₱75 for adults and ₱50 for children, students, seniors and people with disabilities. Verify at the door. The upper floor is reached by stairs, so the house is not step-free. When you leave, San Agustin Church is directly across the street, about ninety metres south.
stops.entranceFeeNote: About ₱75 for adults, ₱50 for children under 18, students, seniors, people with disabilities and government employees; bring valid ID for the discount. Verify at the door.
stops.openingHours: Tuesday to Sunday, 9am to 6pm, last entry 5pm; closed Mondays. Confirm on the day, since it closes for private events.
stops.accessibility: Not step-free: the ground-floor patio and zaguan are level, but the furnished rooms are upstairs and reached only by a staircase.
stops.insiderTip: Look up at the ceilings and window frames rather than the furniture: the capiz-shell window panes, the sliding ventanillas below them and the wooden persianas louvres are the house's real engineering, built for heat, glare and earthquakes.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the courtyard, turn right and cross General Luna Street; San Agustin Church is directly opposite, about ninety metres south, with its heavy adobe façade and the museum entrance beside it.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: San Agustin Church
stops.narration:
This is the oldest stone church in the Philippines, and the only building of its kind in Intramuros to have come through the twentieth century. Look at it before you go in. The walls are adobe — a volcanic rock, quarried for this church at Meycauayan, Binangonan and San Mateo — and they are enormously thick, with buttresses built to take the sideways shove of an earthquake. That engineering is why San Agustin is still here: it survived the great quakes of 1863 and 1880 that felled the cathedral and half the city, and it survived the 1945 bombing that flattened everything around it.

The story begins in 1571, when the Augustinians — the first religious order in the islands, here since 1565 — built a church of bamboo and nipa on this spot. It burned in 1574. A second wooden church burned in 1583, when a candle set fire to the drapery on a governor-general's funeral bier. The Augustinians took the hint and built in stone. Construction began in 1586 to a design by Juan Macías and was completed on 19 January 1607. In 1993 it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list as one of the four Baroque Churches of the Philippines — with Paoay, Santa Maria and Miagao — the country's first World Heritage cultural sites.

Go in, and look up. The ceiling is not carved. It is flat, painted in trompe-l'œil — an optical illusion of three-dimensional mouldings, rosettes and sunken panels — by two Italian painters in the 19th century. Everything else is real: the baroque pulpit with the native pineapple carved into its panels, the choir stalls of dark molave hardwood inlaid with ivory, sixteen crystal chandeliers shipped from Paris, and the pipe organ. Near the high altar is the tomb of Miguel López de Legazpi, the first Spanish governor-general, who died in 1572 — the man who took Maynila and made it Manila. Along the walls and set into the floor are the tombs of governors, soldiers and, later, artists and writers. The church has been a burial place for four centuries.

It has also been a place of horror. In February 1945, during the Battle of Manila, Japanese troops turned the church into a holding camp and kept hundreds of Intramuros residents and clergy inside while the fighting raged; many were killed. The church itself came through with its roof damaged, but the adjoining monastery was destroyed. In the 1970s the monastery was rebuilt as the San Agustin Museum, designed by the architect Angel Nakpil, and it now holds one of the country's finest collections of colonial religious art — vestments, gold vessels, ivory carvings and manuscripts.

Practicalities, because they trip people up. The church is free to enter for Mass, and Masses are held daily; outside service times, the way in is through the museum ticket desk next door, which charges around ₱200 for adults with discounts for students, seniors and children — verify at the door. San Agustin is a popular wedding venue, so on some afternoons the nave closes to visitors for a ceremony; if the doors are shut, come back later or walk the museum instead. Dress modestly, and remember this is an active parish, not a monument.

When you leave, turn south down General Luna and walk about five hundred metres, past the ruins and the schools, to the corner of Muralla and Santa Lucia streets. The gate ahead, set into a garden, leads onto the southern wall at the Baluarte de San Diego.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free to enter for Mass; outside service times entry is through the San Agustin Museum ticket desk next door, about ₱200 for adults with discounts for students, seniors and children. Verify at the door, and check the church is not closed for a wedding.
stops.openingHours: Open for daily Mass and roughly 8am to noon and 1pm to 6pm for museum visitors, Tuesday to Sunday in practice. Closed to tourists during weddings and services. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: The church nave is level and step-free, but the adjoining museum is a converted monastery with stairs, uneven floors and a crypt; the full circuit is not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Stand under the painted ceiling and check whether you can tell it is flat: the trompe-l'œil carving is an illusion by two Italian painters. Then find the pineapple carved into the baroque pulpit — a native fruit worked into Spanish sacred art.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the church, turn south down General Luna Street and walk about five hundred metres, past the ruins and the schools, to the corner of Muralla and Santa Lucia streets. The gate ahead, set into a garden, leads onto the southern wall at the Baluarte de San Diego.

stops.name: Baluarte de San Diego
stops.narration:
You have reached the southern tip of the walled city, standing on the oldest fortification in Intramuros. This bastion, shaped like the ace of spades in a deck of cards, was built around an even older structure: a circular stone watchtower called Fort Nuestra Señora de Guía, designed by the Jesuit priest and architect Antonio Sedeño and finished in 1587 — the first stone fort in Manila. The bastion around it was completed between 1653 and 1663. It has been breached by British cannon fire in 1762, wrecked by the 1863 earthquake, abandoned, and buried under soil during the American period — which is the only reason the round tower underneath survived the 1945 bombing. Archaeologists dug it out between 1979 and 1982, the whole site was restored by 1992, and in 2014 it was declared a National Cultural Treasure.

Stand on the wall and look outward, and you can read the city's whole defensive idea. The walls of Intramuros were begun in 1590 under Governor-General Gómez Pérez Dasmariñas, engineered by Leonardo Iturriano and built by Chinese and Filipino labourers out of the same volcanic tuff quarried at Guadalupe, in today's Makati. The circuit runs for roughly four and a half kilometres and encloses just two-thirds of a square kilometre — a small, dense, walled town of palaces, churches, monasteries, schools and courtyard houses. Outside the wall was a moat, and beyond it the bay. Both are gone: the Americans drained the moat and turned it into a golf course, which still wraps around the walls, and land reclamation for the port pushed the sea away. The city that was a fortress by the water now sits inland.

Then comes the reckoning. This ground was destroyed. In February and March 1945, American and Filipino forces fought Japanese troops for the city street by street — the worst urban battle American forces fought in the Pacific, and one of the most destructive of the whole war. The Japanese naval commander in Manila, Rear Admiral Sanji Iwabuchi, refused his orders to withdraw and fought to the death; the fighting, and the American artillery and bombardment that dislodged him, levelled Intramuros. At least one hundred thousand civilians were killed in Manila that month. After the battle, six hundred bodies were found around these walls. Seven churches stood inside Intramuros; only San Agustin, which you just visited, was left standing. The government, the religious orders, the schools and the wealthy families moved out, and for decades the walled city was a ruin with a golf course and a few residents.

The recovery has been slow and unfinished. The Intramuros Administration was created in 1979 to restore and manage the district; the walls, gates and bastions were rebuilt; a few museums opened; but many of the great buildings are gone for good, and you will notice modern offices sitting where colonial palaces stood. That is the honest state of the place: a fragment, preserved and reconstructed, inside a city of twenty-five million that long ago moved its money and its government to Makati and Quezon City. About seven thousand people live inside these walls today.

So finish here. You have walked from the fort at the river mouth to the southern bastion — the whole Spanish empire in Asia in a kilometre and a half, from conquest to catastrophe to reconstruction. Sit in the garden among the ruins for a few minutes. Then, when you leave, a calesa — a horse-drawn carriage — is often waiting near the gate, and jeepneys and taxis run along the roads outside the walls; Rizal Park and the National Museum complex are just beyond them. If you have a second day in Manila, spend it there: the man whose footsteps you followed at Fort Santiago is buried at the far end of that park, under the Rizal Monument.
stops.entranceFeeNote: A small entrance fee applies; the Intramuros Administration publishes the hours but not the current rate online, so check at the gate. It has recently been in line with the other Intramuros sites, around ₱75 for adults and ₱50 for students, seniors and people with disabilities.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, roughly 8am to 5pm, with last entry at 4pm. Confirm on the day, since the garden closes early for private events.
stops.accessibility: Partly accessible: the garden paths are level, but the bastion itself is reached by steps and the stone surfaces are uneven and unguarded at the edges.
stops.insiderTip: Walk to the outer edge and look down: the round tower at the centre is the excavated 1587 fort, and the grassy ground wrapping the walls beyond is the old moat, drained by the Americans and turned into the golf course you can still see.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Sit in the garden, then leave through the gate onto Muralla Street. A horse-drawn calesa is often waiting nearby, and jeepneys and taxis run along the roads outside the walls. Rizal Park and the National Museum complex are just beyond them, a short ride or a fifteen-minute walk to the south.
